I do not know why the report of the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States is not to be found in the Library of Parliament. It is an important volume and should be available. I would direct the attention of the minister to a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press which I shall read. It was handed to me on the train, when I was returning from the West during the Easter recess, by an English medical doctor who has been travelling in Canada. This gentleman, whose card I have, is Dr. Charles Hawkins, and the cable despatch from London, dated March 31, which he brought to my attention, reads:
The Canadian steamship companies here say that they are receiving from 12 to 15 cancellations daily for passages to Canada, which
[Mr. Calder. J
have been booked by prospective emigrants from the British Isles, the reason given being the continuation of the restriction requiring the increased amount of landing money, which was recently decided upon by the Canadian cabinet. The Canadian immigration authorities here are said to favor this action in so far as it affects continental immigration, but it would appear that it might well be modified in the case of Britishers. It hits hardest those who had booked their passages and made their arrangements before the landing money requirement was altered. Now some of these people find that they cannot go and hence are cancelling their passages daily, much to the discomfiture of the Canadian railway and steamship companies.
Dr. Hawkins told me that he had positive knowledge of a great many immigrants who were cancelling their passages to Canada and who he assured me were agriculturists and farm labourers. Instead of coming to Canada they were re-booking their passages to Australia. I see the minister smiles; no doubt he knows all about it. Well, if such is the case, I think it is most unfortunate that we should lose immigrants of this class. In my opinion, if the British agriculturist and farm labourer have not even $25 in their possession we should welcome them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I may interrupt the
hon. member, I can save the time of the committee. The $250 that we require of immigrants is not asked for in the case of agriculturists and agricultural labourers. No farmer, farm labourer, or domestic coming to Canada is required to have $250.

To what class does the
regulation apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To skilled and unskilled labour, particularly the artisan class.
May I ask then how this information has got abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You see some funny things in the press at times.
Hear, hear.

I have this
gentleman's card here and he assures me this is quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He was absolutely mistaken.

I must take the minister's word and I am glad to hear him make the statement. I was very' much surprised at what was told me. There is another matter to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister. I have here a booklet published by J. Obed Smith in which he makes the statement that immi-

grants coming to Canada cost us $6 per head. Does the minister confirm that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should put it for last year at $5.

That is a very low figure, but does the minister deduct the emigrants that we lose to the United States? That would make a different showing altogether, would it not? Mr. Smith, our immigrant official in the Old Country, makes some very good recommendations in the booklet to which I have already referred, which no doubt the minister has read. Mr. Smith states that after our immigrants land at the port of debarkation the train accommodation is very often not what it ought to be. I know that thirty-nine years ago the accommodation on the railway was not what it should have been and I speak from experience. Mr. Smith also recommends that on every one of our immigration cars, usually known as colonist cars, an official should be placed, and I think the recommendation is a very good one. Perhaps the minister will see what can be done in that direction so that our immigrants shall' not be preyed upon at very many stations where they stop to purchase goods. Furthermore, when our immigrants reach the city of Winnipeg they are turned loose very often. I would like to ask the minister if he has any policy whereby the immigrants can be taken care of from the time they leave the port of debarkation until they reach their destination-whether they are going to work for some farmer or whether they are going to locate right away on land either purchased or homesteaded. Does not the minister think some improvement can be effected along the line of taking care of our immigrants, something of a similar nature to that which has been adopted by the Soldier Settlement Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would be only too glad to put into operation a whole series of improvements I have in mind along these lines. No person comprehends the necessity or value of that more than I do; but again I would say that these things cost money. On the one hand you have members of Parliament complaining most bitterly of the increased cost of government, the increased expenditures, and so on. There are very many improvements that could be made in many departments of government but, I say again, they cost

money. Now to put into being an organization that will look after the immigrant who comes into Canada, in every province of the Dominion, follow him up, see that he is placed, and all that sort of thing, would mean a staff of one hundred or probably one hundred and fifty. These people scatter all over the Dominion, and to follow them through on every train, see that they are properly placed on farms, in factories, and elsewhere, see if they are contented, and all that sort of thing, would necessitate a staff of one hundred or one hundred and fifty and the cost to the country for salaries alone would reach probably $150,000 or $200,000. A very good thing -very helpful and good for the immigrant and for Canada-but, I say again, it costs money. If the House is prepared to vote the money for such a purpose, and for other work as well, I would be only too glad.

Better to spend money
for that purpose than to give it to the provinces to spend for roads.

As a business proposition I would draw the minister's attention to the larger flow of immigrants from Canada to the United States as compared with the flow of immigrants from the United States to Canada. The net loss for the year 1918-19 was in round numbers 52,000, and for the year 1919-20 approximately 95,000. If these immigrants only cost us $5 or $6 a head they are well worth keeping in the country, especially when we realize the high value placed by the Canadian Pacific Railway on a farmer or immigrant who settles along any of its lines of railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not going to question the figures given by my hon. friend -they have been discussed backwards and forwards every year for the past ten years. There would be only one way probably of finding out the truth and that is by the census. When the census is taken we will know exactly what the figures are-we will have our immigration figures for the last ten years, and we shall know as to whether or not these figures are correct. Looking at the position in Canada to-day, in so far as the urban population is concerned, does my hon. friend mean to say there has been a decrease in that population? There is no city in Canada that is not overcrowded to the extent that people cannot get houses to live in. Take the situation as regards the rural population of Canada. There

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: have been here and there certain decreases; but I doubt very much if, on the whole, the rural population of Canada has decreased in the last decade. I say that on the whole you will find places where there has been some decrease, I daresay there has been a change in the proportion between the rural and the urban population; but if you will take our total rural populations as shown at the last census I doubt very much, when we ascertain what the new figures are, if you will find any material discrepancy there.
There is the natural increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it will be found that there is a very material increase.
I said there has been a natural increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Oh, more than the
natural increase because you can estimate that. As regards our urban population, our cities, throughout Canada from coast to coast, are simply teeming with people- they simply cannot find places to live in.' So I say, there is only one way eventually whereby we will be able to check up these increases and that is through the census in both countries.

I wish to ask the minister whether he, as Minister of Immigration, and the Government, have considered a vigorous immigration policy whereby selected immigrants may be placed along the line of the national railways and if so has he anything to say with regard to it?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of course our whole
policy, in so far as agriculturists are concerned, is to bring as many of that class as possible to Canada. We have not, I may say, directed our attention to placing these people along the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern railways here in Ontario-that has not been done.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That has not been done with the exception of certain people who came from the eastern part of the United States, a number of French Canadians, who are being repatriated. Many of them have gone up into those northern regions, but outside of that we have not directed our attention along those particular lines.

I did
not mean particularly along the lines of railway in the province of Ontario; I had reference to the western provinces also. Would not such a policy be worthy of the serious consideration of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

I would like
to draw the minister's attention to the work done in the early eighties by the colonization companies in the western provinces, or what at that time the North West Territories. I was one of the immigrants who settled upon the land as a result of colonization work of this kind, and I know that these companies did very good work indeed. Of course some of them were not a success; but the York Farmers' Colonization Company, of which the minister has no doubt heard, occupied itself with settlement in the Yorkton district. Such a company as that was a very great benefit to the settlers, and its local agent helped them in the purchase of their supplies. Such a company as that was of very great benefit to the settlers. They were also given local land agents, and the settlers were able to make their homestead entries right in the township where they made their selection. I know of some immigrants who settled outside what was at that time known as the Yorkton land district, and they had to go all the way to Regina, or Pile o'Bones, as it was known then, to make their entries, a distance of 135 miles. If some such scheme as that was evolved, I am sure that benefits would result in our favour. Just a word about our immigration officials who work on the trains. I presume they meet the trains at the border coming in from the United States. They must travel back on the trains, say, from Winnipeg as one point, to meet the trains again. If they worked on the trains incoming, why could they not check up the people on the outgoing trains? That may be possible.	.
Can my hon. friend give the figures of the total immigration during the last decade?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I gave figures to the
House for the five-year periods from 1896 down to 1911, then for the three following years and for the last three years. Those figures will all be found in Hansard.
I shall look them up.

I should like to take advantage on this item, Mr. Chairman, of

the invitation extended by the minister to discuss generally the question of immigration and to put forward certain views which I hold and which I believe are held by a great many people in this country. Immigration is a very large question, for the reason that some nine million of us occupy a country which is over three million seven hundred thousand square miles in area, and we are distributed in a most extraordinary fashion, for we occupy a ribbon of territory not more than 300 miles wide at any point stretching from coast to coast. And this great country is capable of maintaining without difficulty a population of two or three hundred million people. If we are to become a great nation we must have population. On the other hand, many people regard unrestricted immigration, particularly of foreigners, with grave apprehension. The question is viewed from four standpoints-the sentimental, the patriotic, the humanitarian, and the material. While some hold that it is dangerous to allow too many foreigners to come in, there are others who take the humanitarian view that we have no right to restrict immigration into a country of such vast area and such boundless natural resources, especially while other countries are overcrowded and congested. And there are those who take the material point of view, that for the purpose of exploiting our resources and developing the country the more immigrants we bring in the better. A variety of causes superinduce immigration, being chiefly the following: industrial depression, political oppression, religious persecution, poverty at home, and prosperity here, the solicitation of friends and relations here, employment agencies, facility of transport, solicitation of steamship companies, assisted emigration, and epidemics.
In considering the people who come to this country of foreign blood, we have to consider them in the light of possible amalgamation in the future or immediate assimilation. Amalgamation is defined as that process which occurs when, by reason of proximity, nations grow together by intermarriage, a process which takes hundreds of years. The best example of this is perhaps the British race itself, the last immigrants having arrived in the British Isles somewhere about 1066. The process of amalgamation has gone forward steadily and as a result a type has been produced. We are not particularly concerned for the next two or three hundred years at least with the process of amalgamation, but we are concerned with the process of assimilation, which is defined as that process whereby immigrants may learn to speak our language, understand our customs, and the working of our political machinery, whereby they may take their places with us upon terms of equality. But it may be laid down that the process of assimilation is rendered slow and difficult or quick and easy precisely in the proportion which the foreign element bears to the British element. That, I think, is fairly obvious. If we have one foreigner living among four men of British blood,-surrounded, so to speak, by men of the British race-the process of assimilation will be quick and easy; but if we have, say, two foreigners, to three men of British blood the process is slower, and the number that can be assimilated is necessarily smaller, until the time might come when by the increase of the percentage of persons of foreign birth the process of Canadianization might come to a standstill, and that of "foreignization" might begin.
I recognize the virtues of the foreigners who have come to us in the past, particularly those who settled upon the western prairies and who came to us with practically nothing but their ability to work. They have made a great success, they have increased agricultural production, and they are slowly but surely climbing up the social and cultural ladder. But there are certain statistics which cannot be denied, and I desire to place them upon Hansard because I believe they are worthy of study by our people. Contrasting these figures with those of the previous decade, which showed a falling off in the numbers of persons of British and French descent and a substantial increase in the number of persons of foreign descent, it is reasonable to assume that the census of 1921 will disolose that there has been a still further falling off of the British element in this country with a very substantial increase of the foreign element.

Of course
my hon. friend recognizes that the war was a potent influence in producing the results shown by his figures.

There has been some discussion of a policy of immigration, and as to the cost of immigration, and so on. I believe it will be admitted by all concerned that our problem is not a problem of getting people to come here, for the whole world is willing to come to Canada if it can get here; our problem is cautiously to admit those who are fit to come here. In an article by Kenneth L. Roberts in the Saturday Evening Post of a few days ago, there is a long discussion of the situation in Europe, and its effect on immigration to the United States:	I am told that the United States
has just recently passed a law, or is about to pass a law, restricting the number of immigrants admitted to that country to 365,000 per year. There can be only two forms of restriction; restriction by numbers, and restriction by classification or qualification. It may happen, and it probably will, that restriction by classification or qualification will in the end produce numbers that we did not expect, and that we shall be unable to deal with. I shall just read the concluding paragraphs of this article I have referred to.
"All of the lines", he told me early in 1921, "are preparing- for greatly increased emigrant business. In the spring they are going to tap new districts for passengers. They are preparing additional emigrant hotel, barrack and quar-anntin e-station facilities. These preparations are based on urgent messages from their agents in all the countries.
"As soon as Germany and Austria are opened for emigration the present flood will be'greatly increased. When Russia is opened, then will come the deluge. The people who are coming are the lowest type of humanity that Europe can send. America has got to keep them out or suffer bitterly in the future."
Americans in Europe are warning their country against the classe of people that are pouring into it, just as they warned it that typhus would break out if a strict quarantine was not imposed. They know the situation, and every word of their warnings is true.
The warnings can never be made strong enough, because of the gravity of the situation and the limitations of the English language.
If no emergency exists for America in respect of immigration, the America that exists to-day is vastly different from the America of ten years ago.
In other parts of the article the writer goes on to describe the mental, moral and physical condition of these millions of people who are clamouring to get to this country if that be possible.
As a result of a study of these figures, I have reached certain conclusions. As I said at the outset, the process of amalgamation does not interest us at the moment. What we are interested in is the process of assimilation. I have adverted to the danger of bringing to this
[Mr. Griesbaoh.'l
country people unacquainted with our system of government, with our institutions and our ideas, and placing our resources and the control of government in their hands. That is a project that is fraught with danger, and my view is this: I think we ought to fix a definite ratio, based on statistics, and we ought no to exceed that ratio. We can restrict either by numbers or by classification and qualification, but no matter by which method we seek to accomplish our end, the Government should have power arbitrarily to decide the moment when that limit is reached, and thereafter we should stand fast and deal with the situation as we have it, until it is dealt with completely. In the determination of this ratio, and in the process of assimilation, we shall have to consider as factors whether we are going to continue the policy of the past, which is the policy of standing still and doing nothing to educate or assimilate the foreigner, or whether, on the other hand, we shall adopt some comprehensive scheme of education which will aid the process of assimilation. If we decide that we shall do no more than we have done in the past, then the ratio we shall decide upon will be a certain figure. On the other hand, if we decide that we will undertake the forced assimilation of the foreigner by a process of education, then, of course, we can raise the ratio or the standard of qualification which may be decided upon.
In my judgment, we cannot look forward to an increased foreign immigration, based upon the figures which I have given, without grave apprehension and misgiving. We cannot look forward to an increased foreign immigration with any degree of satisfaction unless, in the first place, it is controlled and restricted, and unless, in the second place, we adopt a great nation-wide, all-embracing system of education, backed by all the power of the State. Last year I discussed this question very briefly in passing, and now I would say that I know of no plan or scheme of education that has been put forward which will assist or aid in assimilation save one. The churches are practically powerless; our educational system gets us nowhere; there is no plan before this country except the one I have mentioned which begins to measure up to the magnitude or importance of the task. The system which I would lay before the committee-a conclusion which I have arrived at quite independently of the solution itself, and based merely on these figures- is the plan of universal military service

which I laid before the House last year. There you have a scheme which is nationwide, all-embracing, and backed by the supreme power of the State. From the operation of this system no person can escape. You would take your young foreigner at the age of 19, and at the ages of 19, 20, 21 and 22, four years, you would give him three months of military training each year, during which time he would learn to speak our language, keep himself clean, be obedient, and become disciplined. The duties of citizenship and its responsibilities would be impressed upon him, also the fact that he might some day be called upon to defend this country. There you have a system, and the only system that has been proposed, which I believe can adequately or effectively deal with this great problem of keeping the people of this country true to the ideals and traditions which have brought us thus far.
This is a great question. Our actions in this decade are more or less irrevocable. We cannot in this matter of the movement of people and population undo tomorrow what we may do to-day. Therefore, for the future happiness and greatness of this nation, let us hope that in this great matter we come to-day to a right conclusion.

The minister mentioned a few moments ago that he had been looking after colonization on the Transcontinental, and had expended a certain amount of money in the movement of French Canadians from the Eastern States and from the eastern part of the province of Quebec to the Transcontinental. I should like to ask the minister what part he has had in settling that section of the Transcontinental known as the Abitibi country. What assistance has he given to the colonization departments of the Quebec and Ontario Governments in locating settlers along the Transcontinental system in Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have not given any direct assistance. In the eastern part of the United States we have our agencies at two centres, Manchester and Biddeford, where there is a fairly large French Canadian population that has been there for some years. Our officers at those two points have been in touch with the people, and, while I do not know the exact details, I have no doubt that hundreds if not thousands of people have been induced to return to Canada, some of whom doubtless must have been directed to those regions in Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec.

Has the minister ever
been to the Northern Quebec district?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I asked the minister last
year if he would be good enough to make a visit to Northern Quebec and I think he promised me at that time that he would make an effort to do so. The Department of Immigration seems to be at a standstill; so far as colonization is concerned it certainly is absolutely stagnant. There is an opportunity in Northern Quebec, and in Northern Ontario as well, for the execution of a vigorous colonization policy as well as for active work in regard to immigration, for the figures which the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) has given are adverse to Canadian immigration. As the hon. member pointed out, we are losing more people than we are getting. We have been bringing in people for the last fifty years at a great cost to Canada, and we have not only lost every last man, woman and child of them, but we have also lost a portion of the Canadian people as well. We have lost more Canadians, either native born or those who came and settled in Canada, than we have brought to the country in that time, and the vital statistics will substantiate that statement. Within the last forty or fifty years, I venture to say, we have not retained our natural increase in Canadian population. There must be something wrong. In the period from 1901 to 1911 we made quite an advance in immigration and, as the minister is well aware, in colonization as well; but I do not believe we have made any progress in colonization since the close of that period, and we certainly made none previous to that time. During that period a policy was in vogue which aimed at bringing in to Canada, and putting on the land, all the people that we could get. But the Government since that time have adopted a different system. If the minister will go to the Abitibi country, as it is his duty to do, or, at least, if he will send his officials there to make a study of the conditions and the opportunities for settlement, he will be doing as good work for Canada as he canr possibly do in any other direction. There is abundant opportunity in that district for the French Canadian settler to take up land, because the country appeals to him and he likes it. But he is not given a fair chance; he is not given the encouragement which he should have. The French Canadian is the - only man that will settle in Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec,

and until we settle these districts our Transcontinental railway will be a failure.
Until you settle the great districts which are in need of population in Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces, you will continue to have railway difficulties. We have the land, the resources and the opportunities; all we need is a Minister of Immigration and Colonization with courage and foresight, a man who is anxious to bring people into the country and settle them on the land. The minister with such enterprise would render a great service to the country. But instead of that, the minister tells us, in so many words, that his time is taken up in keeping people out of the country; his remarks the other day were tantamount to that. There are thousands of people who want to come into Canada, but apparently the minister thinks it advisable to keep them out. He did not mention anything about a colonization policy, and in answer to an hon. member on the other side this afternoon, he made a statement to the effect that he had made no attempt at colonization in our northern country. The result of his policy and the general policy of the Government has been to drive people out of Canada. Every few days you may pick up the papers and find something about the Mennonites, or some other class of people in Western Canada, trying to locate elsewhere because they are not treated properly in Canada. They are living up to the understanding they had with the Government when they came in, but the Government of the day are not even attempting to fiulfil their end of the agreement. While it might not be desirable to bring in Mennonites, or Hutterites, or Doukhobors, or Galicians in numbers out of proportion to the balance of the population, yet I claim that they are good settlers and producers and would become good Canadians if given a chance. If my hon. friend had a policy to bring in people from Great Britain and the United States, and desirable people from Europe, and had some policy for their assimilation in Western and Northern Canada, he would at once be increasing the population of the country and adding to its productive capacity. Every man who has given any study to the railway problem to-day realizes that our greatest need, if we are to solve our difficulties, is a progressive immigration and colonization policy. It goes without saying that if the land tributary to the railways is not producing anything the railways cannot pay, and my hon. friend a few days ago held out no hope of any 	'
immigration or colonization. It seems to me that the minister simply throws up his hands and bewails the fact that he is helpless. Well, in that regard he is pretty much in the same position as the rest of the Governemnt; he is in good company. I wonder if his attention has been drawn to an article in MacLean's Magazine, by Fred V. Seibert, B.A.Sc., who deals with the colonization problem in Canada? This gentleman, apparently, has been in the Survey Department for some years and has given considerable study to the land settlement question in Canada. On page 8 of MacLean's Magazine for April, 1921, he says:
Settlement needs directing force. There is weakness in our present system and urgent need of control to correct that weakness.
The article is well worth the attention of the minister, who should give more serious study to the question of immigration, and particularly of colonization. His time would be very much better occupied in a close study Of these questions than in playing politics, because his political career, so far as the Government at least is concerned, is very nearly at an end. He could, however, make for himself a reputation as Minister of Immigration and Colonization if he set himself to the task. If the minister has no policy in regard to immigration, then we are to assume that the present muddled condition of our railways will continue, and it will be impossible for us to overcome our railway difficulties, and, in a few years, utterly impossible to pay our taxation and meet our other heavy obligations. There are thousands of people who would come to Canada and make good citizens, and when the minister says that there is no more homestead land I am afraid he is giving Canada rather bad advertising, because there are millions of acres of land that would be suitable for settlement in Western Canada and in Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec. And if it is necessary to build a few branch line railways to develop that country, I think the investment might be considered a good one. But the indiscriminate settlement of homesteaders is a policy I do not believe in. I am not now advocating the continuance of the policy of homesteading at all; a better policy might be worked out. I am satisfied that we could get hundreds of thousands of good people from the United States and across the seas who would make splendid settlers in this country and who would help discharge our burden and pay our interest charges and taxation for the next few years. I ex-

hort the minister to turn his attention more seriously to these important questions than he has done in the past.

I am surprised to hear
the statements of the last speaker in regard to Northern Ontario. I think he has not been up in that part of the country or he would not have such a doleful tale to tell. He has found fault with the minister because there are no immigrants or other persons going into that country. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that I visited that part of Ontario twice during the last ten years and I noticed that a very great improvement had taken place. At New Liskeard a very fine town has sprung up. Within a radius of fifty or a hundred miles of Matheson and Cochrane, the country is very well settled. The hon. member (Mr. Cahill) has always a doleful tale to tell about something, and he may as well talk, about this subject as anything else. He talks about Doukhobors and the like. There is no need to get Doukhobors to settle that country; any amount of good people are going in there-going about as quickly as they possibly can, and that is fairly quick too. I want to tell my hon. friend that there is a fine section of country up there, and ultimately it will be equal to some of the best districts in the older parts of Ontario. I would advise the hon. gentleman to try and assist the minister and the authorities to get people to settle in that northern country and not run it down.

I cannot allow that
statement to pass unchallenged. I did not run the -country down, I praised it very highly.
Now, take your medicine.
I do not wish to be misrepresented.

I have sat and listened
to you time and time again and you were never happy unless you were abusing somebody.
Abusing the Government.

Yes, and I am going to
abuse you and you will have to take it like a man. You are like myself; you are good natured enough and you are not going to get vexed about it. I say:	Be a man and
help Canada all you possibly can; let us all work together shoulder to shoulder and then we will make a success of the development of this country. If we all do what we ought to do, we will make New Ontario a fine part of this Dominion. I do
not like to hear any man run down his country; I do not like a bird that befouls its own nest.

When did the election take place in St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think about September 20, 1920.

I would like to ask
my hon. friend if he belongs to the firm of Nagle & Wigmore?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I did; I was a member.

Is the hon. gentleman still a member?
'Mr. WIGMORE: No.
Until when was he a member of that firm?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Until-the exact date I could not say-within three months ago.
In his dual capacity of Minister of Customs and member of the firm of Nagle & Wigmore, did the hon. gentleman write any letters concerning the business of his firm?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the item under discussion is an item in connection with the Estimates. I do not know that my hon. friend's question has anything to do with the business before the House. I ask for your ruling, Mr. Chairman.
I think I am within the rules in questioning the hon. gentleman as regards the administration of his department.

Before the minister
rose I was about to rise myself. I must say that the questioning of the hon. gentleman seemed to me to be most intimately personal. I have no idea what he is driving at but I submit to you, Sir, that no minister of the Crown, or no member of the House, should be subjected to personal interrogation regarding his private connections unless such interrogation is preceded by a specific charge of some kind affecting the public interest. If such a charge is made in the usual way by an hon. gentleman, upon his responsibility as a member of the House, then it seems to me that no one can object to the interrogation; but I submit to you, Sir, and to my hon. friend who is doing the interrogating, that it is scarcely fair certainly not to the committee and I hardly think to the minister him-se^f to pursue these questions without we on both sides of the House knowing the object, and the purpose, and the basis of the personal interrogations.

I would ask the hon. member for Maisonneuve, if he is going to pursue this course of interrogation any further, to show what bearing it has upon the Estimates in question. If he is leading up to some question bearing on the Estimates, then I do not think that he would be out of order.

Mr. Chairman, we are studying the various items of the Customs Department, and that department is under the direction of the hon. minister who is in his seat. What I wish to call his attention to is the fact that he should do one thing or the other-either attend to the business of the department solely, or to his private business, but not use the Customs Department as a means to advertise his own firm. If the Chairman rules that the question is out of order, there are other means to bring it before the House, but I believe that as we are dealing with the Customs Department, I have the right to question the mode of administration pursued by the

hon. gentleman. This is what I wanted to refresh the memory of the minister for, Mr. Chairman. I am informed that since the hon. gentleman took over the administration of his department he has been writing letters right and left in order to promote the business of the firm to which he belongs. To be fair to him, I will read the letter I have in my hand.
Order.

I first asked him on what date he had taken charge of the department. He said it was in the month of July, that his re-election took place in September, and that he severed his connection with his firm a few weeks ago.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order before the hon. gentleman reads this letter. Just before you took the Chair I had drawn to the attention of the Chairman who preceded' you (Mr. Douglas) that my hon. friend was pursuing a series of quite intimate personal questions-
It is a public, not a personal question.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve "was putting a series of interrogations to the Minister of Customs of a very intimate, personal character.
They refer to the public interest only.

I submit, sir, that before this course is pursued, the hon. gentleman should state clearly the connection between his series of questions and, if I might be permitted to use the word, the insinuations in the form of a charge or a definite statement that there is some public interest involved. I failed to gather from the questions anything relating to the public interest, and I do not think that any minister or member should be subjected to such a cross-examination unless the committee are taken into the confidence of the hon. gentleman as to his reasons for submitting the questions; and, further, I submit that the item under discussion being an item in the Customs Department, this course should not be pursued under it. If my hon. friend considers that the Minister of Customs has in any way used his position improperly, then I submit that a charge should be made and the letter read in that connection, and not placed on Hansard when there is no proper opportunity to deal'with it in a parliamentary manner.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I regret, that I was not in the Chair to hear the preliminary

remarks made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), but from what I have heard upon the point of order,
I would judge that the question is this: Has an hon. member in Committee of Supply the right to refer to any act of a minister of the Crown which does not concern his official conduct as such minister? The doctrine laid down in May's Parliamentary Procedure on that point is quite clear. At page 486, he says:
Regarding the general conduct of debate- in the committee of supply, it may be observed that remarks on the conduct of a servant of the state, made on the grant containing hi-s salary, must be restricted to his official conduct. The committee of supply does not afford the proper opportunity for discussing, whether a minister should be in the cabinet or not.
Anything, therefore, which would concern the official conduct of the minister would be perfectly in order. On the other hand, any complaint which any hon. member might have to make concerning his conduct in relation to his private life or affairs would be more properly made either upon a motion to go into Supply or introduced as a matter of privilege.

Mr. Chairman, the
matter I have to call to the attention of the minister and the committee is one which affects the public interest, and if I were permitted to read the letter which I have in my hand the committee would at once see its relevancy. The letter emanates from the Department of Customs; it is written on the official paper of the department, and in the body of the letter the hon. minister intimates that he writes as Minister of Customs. Therefore, it is in the public interest as it affects the administration of his department. I have no charge to make at present against the minister; that is why I was asking him a few questions. He may have a perfectly satisfactory explanation, of which the committee will be able to judge. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I purpose to read this letter and ask the hon. minister if he admits its authenticity, and what explanation he has to give regarding it. This letter is written on the official paper of the department, and bears the Royal Coat of Arms, it is as follows:
Ottawa, January 13, 1921. French Purchasing Commission,
Care of French Embassy,
London, E.C., England.
Dears Sirs,-I am informed that your Government will have quite a few French steamers taking grain from the port of Saint John N.B. Canada this winter.
The firm of Nagle and Wigmore of which I am a member are very anxious to secure this business. We are the largest firm of shi.pbrokers in Saint John and have done a very large amount of business along these lines.
We have our own tow-boats, tend -to all stevedoring and all matters in connection with the general brokerage business.
As you are no doubt aware, I am Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue in the Canadian Government and I spoke to Sir George Foster, my colleague in the Cabinet who has just returned from England being Canada's representative at the League of Nations' conference which has just been concluded at Geneva and he advised me to write to you.
We are in a position to handle your business to your satisfaction and would refer you to. the Bank of Nova Scotia as to our financial ability.
We are agents for the Canada Steamships Lines Limited, the Compagnie Canadienne Transatlantique, Limited, the Fracanda line and the Acadian Shipping Company Limited.
I would very much appreciate your giving us your business.
Thanking you in anticipation,
I remain,
Yours very truly,
R. W. Wigmore.
Sir, I consider this a matter of public importance, because the hon. minister speaks not only as a member of the firm of Nagle and Wigmore, but as Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; and he refers to an interview he had with one of his colleagues-indeed, the senior member of the Government, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). It is a matter of public interest whether a minister of the Crown has the right to act in this way, using his position to promote the business of a firm with which until a few weeks or months ago he was connected. My object in bringing the matter before the committee is to ascertain whether or not the hon. gentleman admits that he wrote this letter. I would like to have an answer from the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am not surprised
that the hon. member for Maisonneuve has brought this question up, because I heard that he had a copy of this letter and had had a photograph of it made. I want to say, to begin with, that since being called into the Cabinet I absolutely have received no benefit in any way, shape or form, financial or otherwise, from the firm of which I was a member at that time. I wrote this letter not with any understanding that it would benefit our firm personally. I wrote it as I would write a letter on behalf of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve if he were in the business and came to me and asked me if I would write on his behalf to this firm; for if he had done so I certainly would have written a letter on his behalf.

I did not write it with any idea that there was to be any benefit from the Minister of Customs' standpoint, or in any other way, only in writing to this firm in England they would not know who I was and I simply said I was Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue in Canada. I have received no benefit, as I say, in any way, shape or form, financially or otherwise, from the firm of which I was a member at that time. My partner is carrying along the business and I wrote this letter with the idea of securing business for him just as I would to secure business for any other firm that would write to me. We receive letters from day to day asking us to recommend certain firms and certain people, and it was in this way that the letter was written.

I notice that there is one gentleman who applauds. I would like to know if the people of Canada would applaud if they were witnesses to what is taking place this afternoon. The hon. gentleman has made his answer and we must accept it. I do accept it, especially that part of it in which the hon. gentleman admits that he signed this letter and mailed it. All comments are unnecessary. Mr. Chairman, in all the annals of British parliamentary government, either in Canada or in the Mother Country, I challenge any one to find such a glaring example of personal interest mixed with the administration of public affairs. No minister of the Crown, either in Canada or in the Mother Country would ever dare to mix his own personal business with the public business. I dare say that if the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce knew that his name had been mentioned in this letter he would at once have disowned the author of it. It is highly improper for a minister of the Crown to boost his own private business whilst using the royal coat of arms and the official paper of the Government. It is improper per se; then, it is improper so far as it affects his competitors in the city of St. John. It is also improper because the hon. gentleman was competing with the Government of which he is a member, because they also have a merchant marine which can perform the business which the hon. gentleman is seeking for his own firm. Besides, he was practically writing to a foreign government, and that indeed is a sad feature I find in this matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must point out to the hon. member for Maisonneuve that under the rules of the House he is obliged

to accept the statement of the hon. minister that he was not interested in the firm at the time the letter was written.

Well, I accept what the hon. gentleman said, that he wrote the letter. But the letter cannot bear two interpretations. I will read it again. At the top there are the words "Minister of Customs," and immediately underneath, the royal coat of arms. The letter says:
Ottawa, January 13, 1921. French Purchasing Commission,
Care of French, Embassy,
London, E.C,., England.
Dear Sirs:-

I rise to a point of
order. The letter has already been read.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order is well taken. The hon. member certainly has no right to read the letter again.

The minister admits
having written and signed the letter, but he qualifies that statement by saying that he had no personal interest, whereas by the very reading of the letter you can see the interest blazoned across it. He says-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The letter is on Hansard and it speaks for itself. I must rule that the letter cannot be read again.
But I may comment on the letter?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may comment on it, but not read it again.

The hon. gentleman says he has no personal interest. What does he mean when he says in the letter?-
We have our own tow 1 oats, tend to all stevedoring and all matters in connection with the general brokerage business.
As you are no doubt aware I am Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue in the Canadian Government and I spoke to Sir Geo. Foster, my colleague in the Cabinet who has just returned from England, being Canada's representative-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is evading the rule; he is reading the letter again under the guise of commenting upon it. He certainly cannot do that.

I accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman. My comment is that the hon. gentleman as Minister of Customs has written a most improper letter which should arrest the attention of the right hon. leader of the Government. The Minister of Customs in writing this letter promoted his own personal interest or the interest of this firm-
Order.

Well, I accept the
statement he madei. I must accept it, qualified by the terms of the letter. At all events I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister to this question-
I rise to a point of order.
Does he approve of any of his minister's writing such a letter?

My point of order is this. The minister made a statement in reply to the interrogations and the reading of this letter by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), I submit that the hon. member has no right whatever to insinuate or suggest any improper motive on the part of the minister, unless, as I stated before, when I appealed for your ruling, he is prepared, from his seat in the House, to prefer charges of improper conduct against the minister. I submit the hon. gentleman is not in order under the Estimates of this department in pursuing the course that he has pursued.

It is quite obvious that the hon. gentleman is not in sympathy with the minister who wrote this letter, and I do not see why he rises to this point of order. I was simiply asking the leader of the Government if, taking cognizance of this letter, he approves it, and if he does not think that a minister of the Crown who could write such a document does not deserve to remain in the Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether there is a point of order awaiting your decision or not; if there is, I do not wish to intervene. Otherwise, I want to assure my hon. friend that I am not able to be so profoundly moved by the letter to which he refers as he seems to be. The letter which was brought to my attention-I think it must be the letter to which he has referred this afternoon; I do not need to see it- appears to have been a letter written for a firm of which the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue (Mr. Wigmore) had been, or was a member and with which his name was still associated.
He signed it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On behalf of that firm. The only reference in the world to his position is by way of explaining how he comes to write the letter, by reason of his being a colleague of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), and

the matter having been brought to his attention by that minister upon inquiry on his return from overseas. I did not know that it was a penal offence for a man writing a private letter to refer to the fact that he was a minister by way of explaining that the information prompting the letter came from a colleague who happened to have been overseas, and to have learned that this commission, whatever it was, was to have boats running to St. John. I tried to inquire, that is, in my mind, whether or not there could possibly be any motive in it that could be criticized in any way at all; but my imagination or ingenuity was not sufficient to enable me to see how there could be any improper motive. If there had been any way in which, as minister, he could have assisted them, the case might have been different, but there is no way in the world by which he could do that. The hon. gentleman was merely explaining how he came to write the letter; being a colleague of Sir George Foster, Sir George Foster told him that the commission would require this service. The reference was merely incidental; there was no improper thought or improper purpose, either real ' or imaginary. It is not for me to approve or disapprove of conduct particularly, unless such conduct is of a character inconsistent with the duties of the minister as a minister. I must say that I was not able in this case to discern conduct of any corrupt or culpable nature.

I noticed in the press the
other day the retirement of Mr. Belyea. Can the minister give me the details about the retirement of this official from the St. John office?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The amalgamation of
the Departments of Customs and Inland Revenue, not only in St. John, but throughout the Dominion, is in the hands of a committee of the Civil Service Commission, and their report to a subcommittee of the council was that we could dispense with the services of Mr. Belyea in the city of St. John. The positions of Collector of Customs and Collector of Inland Revenue have been amalgamated, and both of them are now in charge of Mr. Lockhart. Mr. Belyea has not been in good health for some time, and he will retire on his regular superannuation allowance.
How does that superannuation allowance compare with the salary which he was receiving?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: His salary was $2,280. He will retire on a superannuation allowance of $1,568.

I have only a slight acquaintance with the gentleman in question, but as regards his age, I thought from his appearance he would be a more likely man to take charge of the combined office than Mr. Lockhart, and that the latter would be more in line for superannuation than Mr. Belyea. I was wondering why Mr. Belyea was selected for retirement.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I know this case very well and I can assure my hon. friend that Mr. Belyea's condition is such that it would be impossible for him to carry on long. I would not like to say here just what that condition is.

He was quite satisfied to
retire, was he?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. He was a much younger man that Mr. Lockhart, but there are reasons why he retired. I will give the information to my hon. friend.

The minister might
give a similar explanation with regard to the Collector of Customs at Pictou, N.S., Mr. R. P. Fraser. I am informed that he was retired. Why was he retired from the Customs Department and another person taken from the Inland Revenue Department and put in his place?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That is a similar case. He was retired by the Civil Service Com-

mission. He was, I believe, 76 years of age. It was found possible to do away with one of the two officers at Pictou. The man succeeding him is 67, a much younger officer. Mr. Fraser will retire on quite a substantial retiring allowance.
Does the minister invariably take the ages of these officials as a qualification?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
No, the Civil Service
Commission handles the matter.

I do not know anything particularly about these two gentlemen. I know that Mr. Fraser is very vigorous and is and always has been a satisfactory officer. It occurred to me that, perhaps, this was pretty cruel treatment to mete out in his old days to a gentleman who was in good health and vigour and able to attend to his office and to his work. He has a large family to support, he is not blessed with too much of this world's goods, and his retiring allowance will not be at all sufficient to meet the necessary requirements of his family. I do not know either of them personally, but this is the information that has been given to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

The retirements are
recommended by the Civil Service Commission, who report to a sub-committee of council. Mr. Fraser was the oldest employee there, and I suppose on that account it was decided that he should be retired.
Who was his succes1-sor?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

Moonshiners.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

I know that there are certain officers in the important centres, but I think there used to be subordinate officers here and all over the country, local men, who went around to see if any illicit manufacturing was being done. They re-

ceived only a small salary. Has the minister such officers in his department now?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

Is it equitable and fair that because he has failed to put in that much longer time he should suffer a reduction? The minister should consider the case of worthy officers who have given their time to the State, and, out of the saving which he contemplates making, he should provide something for cases of that kind, where men have gone out of their ordinary occupations into the service of the country, having unfitted themselves for other work. This seems hard, especially as some of these men have not saved any money out of the meagre pittances they have received from the Government. The salaries in the country do not approximate those paid in Ottawa and the other cities. The men in the country are under paid,

while it might be said that in Ottawa many of them are overpaid. Can the minister really not provide, out of the vast savings he expects to make, something for worthy officers on the outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I agree with the hon.
member that in many cases the recommendations for retirement work a great hardship to certain men, but unfortunately the minister of the department has nothing to do with the matter. These recommendations are made by the Civil Service Commission to a sub-committee of Council and are acted upon accordingly. It does seem unfortunate that a man should not benefit by the amount of retirement that would be given to him if he had served a few days longer than the date of his actual retirement* but the ruling having been laid down I cannot help it.

I wish to take up the
case of Stratford, where the collector of customs is now presumed to take over the offices of both Customs and Inland Revenue. His work is fairly heavy and responsible now. If the collector of customs cannot be given an increase at all, I should like to know whether some representation could not be made to the Civil Service Commission with a view to securing fair play in this matter. What is the revenue at Stratford from customs and inland revenue, and what is the salary paid the officer now conducting both services?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I quite agree that on
amalgamation, particularly of the larger offices, where greater responsibilities are placed on the collectors, and where in some cases it is almost impossible for them to get through with their work, some consideration should be given. It is my intention on the reorganization of the department to make certain recommendations to the Civil Service Commission, who have this matter in hand, so that in those cases where there has really been an extra amount of work placed on these men, the work should be graded differently and some consideration should be accorded them. I assure the hon. gentleman that I will take this matter up with the Civil Service Commission and make a recommendation along those lines. The Customs revenue at this particular port is $185,000.	[DOT]
And the salary is what?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The salary of the collector is $2,160.

I would like to ask the minister a question with regard to the outport
of Strathroy. I notice on page D-43 of the Auditor General's Report the following:
Strathroy:	W. H. Murray, sub-collector,
$1,300 bonus, $396 ; H. W. Paddell, clerk, $1,200, bonus, $396; Miss M. DeCourcy, preventive officer, $850, bonus, $420; G. E. MacKenzle, relieving: officer, 3 m. to Mar. 31, $274.98, bonus, $72.55 ; board, etc., W. J. Element, $32.40 ; postage and p.o. box, $22.25-
Do I understand from this item in the Auditor General's Report that all these officers are stationed at the town of Strathroy, and that they occupy offices, and draw salaries for work performed there?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The headquarters of
that particular district and the chief port is London; Strathroy is just an outport.
I understand that quite well, but I would imagine that if that were the case the salaries of these people would be charged to the city of London. What have they to do with Strathroy?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Nothing at all.
Take Miss DeCourcy; what are her duties in the Strathroy office?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is only one
officer at Strathroy; all the rest are at London. This lady the hon. gentleman speaks of is at London.

Then this item in the Auditor General's Report should not be in the form in which it is, and the salaries of these officers should not be charged to the Strathroy office. Miss DeCourcy, H. W. Paddell and W. J. Element have never been in the Strathroy office.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If the hon. member
will refer to page D-42 of the Auditor General's Report he will find that is all under the chief port of London, the total for salaries being $43,722. The different offices are enumerated, and Strathroy is only an outport.
I understand that quite well. But why should these salaries be charged to the Strathroy office? These people have never entered the Strathroy office in their lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: They are not.

But at page D-43 all these
offices are under the heading of "Strathroy" and their salaries are charged to that office. Mr. Murray is the only officer there.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is something
wrong. They should be under the London office; there is no question about that. There is only one officer at Strathroy.
REVISED EDITIpN.
That is what I was pointing out. From the way the information appears in the Auditor General's Report any person reading it would believe all these persons are stationed at Strathroy.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is a mistake; they
are all stationed at London with the exception of one officer at Strathroy. I think his name is Murray.

I was going to make further inquiry when the member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) intervened with regard to the amount of collections at the port of Stratford. I was going to ask if it is the intention of the minister to recognize the increased responsibilities and work that will devolve upon the collector at the port of Brantford by reason of the amalgamation. My recollection is that the collections in the Customs will amount to a million of dollars almost, and probably $200,000, or perhaps more, in the Inland Revenue. The offices having been amalgamated and it appears to me that the Customs officer, who has now been in the employ of the department several years, would be entitled to further consideration by reason of the vast amount of work that will be put upon him, and the increased responsibilities that the double office will create in the city of Brantford. If the minister has these facts I would like to hear them.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The revenue from
Brantford last year in customs was $900,000, and in inland revenue $175,000. The same statement that I made to the hon. member for Perth, applies in like manner to Brantford or any other place. I believe that these men who have had extra duties placed upon them should receive extra consideration, and my recommendation to the Civil Service Commission will be along that line.
May I ask the number of Customs and Inland Revenue officers in the riding of North Cape Breton and Victoria, and the different places at which they are stationed?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: It will take some little time to look that information up. Will the hon. gentleman tell me to what ports he refers? I have not got them in alphabetical order here, but only by counties.

I think there is a custom house at Cape North, in the northern end of the county. I think there are also customs houses at Neil's Harbour,
[Mr .Wig-more.]
North Ingonish, South Ingonish, English-town, Baddeck, Little Narrows, Iona, Grand Narrows, North Sydney, and Sydney Mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There are fourteen
officers at Baddeck and at out ports. There are fifteen at Northm Sydney and out ports. I will be very glad to read the names of the officers at Baddeck. They are as follows:
D. J. Macrae, Collector of Customs, at Bad-deck ; J. A. Bain, Customs Patrol Officer, New Campbellton ; J. J, Bain, Customs Patrol Officer, New Campbellton; Captain A. Carmichael, Customs Patrol Officer, Munroe's Point; Edward Dowling, Customs Patrol Officer, Neil's Harbour ; John Larusic, Customs Patrol Officer, Aspy Bay ; W. R. McKinnon, Sub-collector of Customs, New Campbellton; Donald McAulay, Customs Patrol Officer, St. Ann's; P. A. Macintosh, Customs Patrol Officer, White Point; D. B. McKay, Customs Patrol Officer, Little Narrow's; Alex. McLeod, Customs Patrol Officer, Engllshtown; Edward Maeneil, Sub-collector of Customs, Iona-
There are a couple of temporary officers :
-T. D. Curtis, Customs Patrol Officer, Ingonish ; Duncan Carey, Customs Patrol Officer, New Campbellton.
The names of the officers at North Sydney are:
Jos. McPherson, Collector; J. H. Cameron, John Cogan, John J. McDonald, David Edwards, P. E. Jackson. H. W. McNeil, Angus Toung, John Boutillier, D. J. McGillivray, Chas. J. K. Jessome, Roderick McDonald, Robert Newton, James Peck, and E. A. McNeil.
Is any provision made for increases to these men from year to year? Some of them are rather old officials and get small pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: No provision is made for increases to these patrol officers. Statutory increases are granted to collectors of customs, and are fixed by the department and the Civil Service Commission.
Were any increases made in the last two or three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Not for those small
offices.
Can the hon. gentleman give the number of port officers for Montreal this year as compared with 1917, 1918, 1919, and 1920?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have not the information here, but last year there were 398 officers in the port of Montreal, and the out-ports connected with it.
And this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I can give the hon. gentleman that information later on.
What were the total salaries paid to those officers? And have any increases been granted?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: The total salaries for 1920 were $511,600. The proposed statutory increases will amount to $17,135.
Will those officers get the bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
What is the customs revenue from the port of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext: What are the Inland Revenue receipts from the city of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have not any statistics.

How many Inland
Revenue officers are employed in the Montreal district?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: About one hundred and four or one hundred and five.

How many seizures
were made by those officers last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext: Has my hon. friend received representations from the Board of Trade and from .the Chamber of Commerce of the district of Montreal as regards the duties levied in view of the premium on the American dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not remember any such representations. I should judge they would get to the Minister of Finance.
Yes. But has any decision been made as regards discrepancy in the duties affected by the premium on the American dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, there is no difference between the standard dollar of Canada and the standard dollar of the United States.

But as a matter of fact there is with the appreciation of the American dollar, and the depreciation of the Canadian dollar. Is not the department by not adjusting this matter giving
the Americans a real preference in shipping their goods here?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Of course, under the present law we cannot make any change. I do not know what may be done in the future.	'

But my .hon. friend can see at once that it works in favour of the American and against the British exporter to Canada. It seems to me that the provisions of the Customs Act with respect to standard currency should be amended in order to give our friends in Great Britain and importers in Canada a chance to compete with the Americans.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Act says:
In computing the value for duty of such currency the rate thereof shall he such as has been ordered and proclaimed from time to time by the Governor in Council who is hereby empowered to make such order.
The rate so ordered shall be based upon the actual value of the standard coins or currency of such country as compared with the standard dollar of Canada in so far as such comparative values are known.

In view of the depreciation of the Canadian dollar on the American market, does my hon. friend not think that an amendment might be introduced to effect an adjustment of things? I am afraid that we shall have to suffer from this depreciation for quite a number of years and the Americans will get the best of us. Canadians will lose the benefit of the British preference because on your Canadian dollar you lose 13 or 14 cents; it has even gone as low as 17.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Of course, this is a question of policy and is a matter for the Finance Minister. I may tell my hon. friend, however, that it has been under consideration for some time.

I would like to ask the minister how he arrives at the total of this vote, $6,782,195, showing an increase of $129,086.75. I find there is an actual decrease of $454,100 from last year's Estimates. Why does this discrepancy exist?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Last year we had two votes, one for the Customs and one for the Excise; this year we are amalgamating the two departments, so there must be some consideration that the hon. member has not taken into account.

I am simply taking the figures as they appear in this Estimate, page 66. I find it difficult to reconcile the amounts as given on this page. Apparently there should be a large decrease in the

amount asked for, whereas there is actually shown an increase.
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I would like to get this item through if possible.
Oh, I think the minister should be satisfied. I would like him in the meantime to consider the last question that I brought up and to be ready to make a statement when we return to his Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is a question for the Minister of Finance.

My hon. friend is administering the Customs Act. At any rate, the matter should be considered either by him or the Finance Minister.
Progress reported.
